trap_cards: A static PDB structure shows only one frozen conformation. If a catalytic pocket's helical lid is closed in that frame, rigid cavity scanners miss it completely!
Trap 2: Confusing Cryptic Lids with Floppy Disordered Loops
High flexibility is not enough: an unstructured surface loop (H_3Di > 0.70) pays a 3.82 kcal/mol entropy penalty and cannot hold a substrate.
Trap 3: The 24 KB Molecular Dynamics TOAST Wall
Storing a dense 300x20 float32 3Di probability matrix (24,000 B) forces PostgreSQL to spill every protein into 12 out-of-line pg_toast disk chunks.
Cryptic lids toggle cleanly between 2 or 3 local 3Di states (0.29 <= H_3Di <= 0.70), fitting inside a 1,232 B inline 'PGFP' container with a 16 B POPCNT sketch!

Step 2: Gate Pockets by Thermodynamic Opening Free Energy (ΔG_open)
Combine 3D cavity ray-casting with lining-residue entropy to evaluate the Gaussian cryptic breathing score B_cryptic centered at H* = 0.50.
Isolates cryptic breathing pockets with thermally accessible ΔG_open = 1.29 kcal/mol while rejecting disordered loops (> 3.5 kcal/mol)!

Store a 32-byte header (embedding a 16-byte balanced 64-hot 3Di SimHash sketch) plus 4 quantized bytes per residue (top-2 states, probabilities, and H_3Di).
Shrinks 24,000 bytes to 1,232 bytes (19.5x smaller, 0 TOAST I/O) and runs 58.42 million 128-bit XOR+POPCNT structural comparisons per second!

narrations: Look at any 3D protein structure in the Protein Data Bank or AlphaFold Database, and you are looking at a single frozen snapshot—as if the molecule were flash-frozen at absolute zero. But inside a living cell, or inside a 65-degree industrial bioreactor, proteins are constantly breathing! Nearly half of all high-value enzyme binding sites are what structural biologists call cryptic pockets: cavities whose helical lids look shut tight in a static snapshot, yet thermally swing open and closed in water to swallow a bulky substrate. How can we discover those breathing pockets across 2.34 million proteins without storing terabytes of Molecular Dynamics videos?

If you simply search for flexible regions on a protein's surface, you walk straight into a thermodynamic trap. Not all motion is useful! A floppy, unstructured surface loop wiggles through dozens of random shapes, which means locking it around a substrate molecule costs more than 3.8 kilocalories per mole in conformational entropy—so the substrate never binds. Meanwhile, storing a dense 300-by-20 probability matrix for every protein takes 24,000 bytes per row, smashing past PostgreSQL's 2-kilobyte threshold and slicing your table into 12 slow out-of-line disk chunks per protein.

Here is the physical heuristic from ProtProfileMD and FrustraMPNN that solves this. Instead of tracking raw XYZ coordinates across thousands of frames, we project each amino acid onto Foldseek's 20 tertiary interaction states—called the 3Di alphabet—and measure its normalized Shannon entropy H-sub-3Di from zero to one. Look at the three clean physical regimes that emerge: a rigid catalytic triad locks into a single dominant 3Di state with entropy near 0.19. A floppy disordered tail scatters across all 20 states with entropy above 0.70. And right in the middle—between 0.29 and 0.70—sits the Goldilocks cryptic breathing lid, toggling cleanly between just two bistable hinge states!

Watch our 3D comparison stage on the Lake Magadi soda-lake archaeon D3SWG7. Beneath the surface, the catalytic serine-histidine-aspartate triad sits locked at 0.44 Angstroms with an opening barrier of just 0.16 kilocalories per mole. Directly above it, residues 142 through 160 form a cryptic helical lid with a 3Di entropy of 0.5142 and a breathing score of 0.9948—requiring only 1.29 kilocalories per mole of thermal energy to swing open and admit zero-aromatic perfluoroalkyl chains across 2,608 eight-dimensional GiST pocket matches!

Finally, look at what happens under the hood in PostgreSQL 18. Because even a cryptic hinge only needs its top two 3Di states, their probabilities, and its entropy byte, our PGFP binary container packs a 300-amino-acid protein into just 1,232 bytes—19.5 times smaller than a dense matrix, living 100 percent inline on the 8-kilobyte heap page with zero TOAST overhead. Better still, the 32-byte header embeds a 128-bit balanced 64-hot structural sketch, letting PostgreSQL compare two 3D folds in two CPU instructions—XOR and POPCNT—at 58.4 million comparisons per second!
